title: Billie Holiday wins the dice game; Lester Young's luck
summary: He tells how Billie Holiday won everyone's money shooting dice on the bus and that Lester Young never won, then returns to the Chick Webb battle of January 1938.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her

blocks.x: She's in the back of the bus. We're coming in and you know how foggy it used to get from Boston coming in. This was at the same time, I'm pretty sure, that we were playing on a Sunday - we were going to play with Chick Webb but they wouldn't tell me this. Now we're coming out of the Christmas - we're coming out of '37, coming out of December going into the first part of January. It was around the Christmas week. Incidentally she broke up everybody. She just took everybody's money because they told her wrong and she shot the dice wrong and broke the whole band. (laughs) You know, if you shoot 12 you win, if you shoot 2, if you shoot 7 - whatever they told her, whatever, she won. This was a very cute thing. This was an inside thing. It's important - you know, you're telling somebody wrong and she don't know what she's doing, but she's winning. She broke everybody.
That's very interesting. I didn't know that Billie Holiday was a southpaw.

She was a southpaw. Jack Washington said, "Get 'em, baby," and I was sitting up in the front and laughing. We got some neck bones and rice and beans and she put the pot on and she told everybody goodnight. You know, she put the money down in her bosom, she wouldn't give Jimmie Rushing no money, she wouldn't speak to Basie. She didn't speak to the bus driver or nobody; she went on around the corner and said, "I'm putting the pot on."

Poor Lester Young always wanted a Packard car and he never did win one. He never made no money the whole time he stayed in Basie's band; he got broke shooting dice. He never could win, but however, back to the serious part of it, I'm pretty sure - because we had done the "Spirituals to Swing" and Benny Goodman was down doing his concert and we were up there doing the battle of music with Chick, and this had to be January 1938. It's got to be that date because Zutty was there, Chick Webb, and it was a thing that we weren't thinking about. All we was thinking about was how many people were going to come in and how much money we were going to split up when we got through. We didn't care who liked what. All we wanted to do was get some gate receipts so we could pay our room rent and take care of our children.
